claims.text: A framework integrating high-throughput anharmonic lattice-dynamics simulations with atomic-scale phonon-scattering descriptors can significantly improve predictions of low lattice thermal conductivity in disordered high-entropy alloys.
The intended materials are near-equiatomic, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys in their as-synthesized state.
The proposed method combines anharmonic lattice-dynamics simulations, first-principles calculations of force-constant fluctuations, and machine-learning regression.
The proposed method is intended to operate from 300 to 700 K under phonon-dominated transport conditions.
The proposed method assumes that the alloys remain in a single-phase disordered state.
Chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys produces force-constant fluctuations.
Atomic-scale disorder enhances anharmonic phonon scattering.
Disorder-induced force-constant variability and scattering reduce phonon lifetimes.
Lattice distortion and enhanced phonon scattering reduce lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Explicitly quantifying force-constant fluctuations and anharmonic scattering in a machine-learning model will improve prediction accuracy relative to conventional methods.
The framework will predict lattice thermal conductivity within ±15% of experimental measurements.
Current lattice-thermal-conductivity models often have errors exceeding 25%.
Existing first-principles and phenomenological approaches do not fully capture disorder-induced anharmonic scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Failure to capture disorder-induced scattering causes significant deviations from experimental lattice thermal conductivity.
The method is expected to apply only to near-equiatomic, disordered high-entropy alloys without substantial ordering or secondary phases.
The method may not be valid for complex multiphase alloys or at extreme temperatures where other scattering mechanisms dominate.
Transferability of the simulated scattering descriptors across diverse high-entropy-alloy systems is uncertain.
The benchmark will compare predicted and experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity at several temperatures from 300 to 700 K.
Experimental lattice thermal conductivity will be measured using time-domain thermoreflectance or laser-flash analysis.
The hypothesis is falsified if measurements consistently deviate by more than ±15% from predictions or if the model fails to capture the temperature dependence of lattice thermal conductivity.
